children: In this case, one out of two is a pretty great result.

SpaceX didn't accomplish all of its goals during the 15th test flight of its Starship rocket, but it still did something amazing. Roughly 23 hours after leaving Earth on Friday evening, the rocket's upper stage returned and was caught by its launch tower.

A Starship spaceship orbiting Earth has returned, with the potential to be used again. That's the first time a spaceship has returned since 2011, when NASA's Space Shuttle returned on its final flight. The Shuttle, however, isn't really a rocket, making Starship's return another first for SpaceX.

(Elon Musk's rocket and AI company also holds the distinction of being the first privately-funded company to reach orbit with a liquid-fueled rocket, the first private company to visit the International Space Station, and the first rocket company valued at north of $1 trillion, among other feats.)

Saturday's event can be rewatched here. Some five million people watched the catch. Images of a glowing ship reentering Earth's atmosphere at more than 26,000 kilometers per hour, engulfed in plasma reaching 7,000 degrees Fahrenheit, were quite something.

Catching the rocket on the launch tower with huge mechanical arms will aid in rapid reusability. Eventually, SpaceX plans to launch Starship thousands of times a year. Today, SpaceX launches its partially-reusable Falcon 9 rocket hundreds of times a year. Falcon 9 carries a majority of the world's cargo into orbit.
SpaceX intended to catch the booster stage and the upper stage during the 15th test flight. The booster autonomously aborted the attempt on Friday after a low fuel warning, according to SpaceX.
While in orbit, Starship deployed another 26 next-generation version-three (V3) Starlink satellites.

Starlink is SpaceX's space-based broadband product serving more than 13 million customers in more than 170 countries, using more than 11,000 satellites. The business generated about $3.5 billion in third-quarter earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (Ebitda), up from $1.9 billion in the third quarter of 2025.
SpaceX deployed 26 V3 satellites during test 14, on Sept. 28. V3 satellites are almost four times the size of V2 satellites, with about 10 times the data transfer capacity.

SpaceX needs Starship to deliver the larger satellites. It also needs Starship for its Starmind AI computing satellites. SpaceX hopes to build an AI data center in space, likely starting in late 2027.

SpaceX stock dipped 2% in after-hours trading on Friday after the failed booster catch attempt. It's hard to say how the stock will react to the test flight on Monday. Whatever happens, catching the upper stage is an amazing accomplishment.

Progress on Starship is critical for SpaceX stock. Starship is the technology that unlocks low-cost data centers in space. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," tweeted Musk on Nov. 4, after Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm elections.

Coming into Monday trading, SpaceX stock was just 3% above its $135 IPO price and down 38% from its all-time high of $225.64 reached shortly after the June IPO. Several factors have weighed on investor sentiment — most related to AI and the risk that industry-wide growth of the new technology will slow.
